## Architecture

A FastAPI + DuckDB API runs in Docker on a VPS (behind Caddy for HTTPS),
**built directly on that VPS** — no container registry, no self-hosted
GitHub Actions runner, no CI permissions to fight with. The static frontend
(HTML/CSS/vanilla JS + Leaflet) is served from GitHub Pages and calls the
API over `fetch()`.

::: {.callout-important}
## Read this before following an older copy of these instructions
An earlier design `COPY`-ed the 17GB `.duckdb` file into the Docker image
(with a separate data image pushed to GHCR, built on a self-hosted Actions
runner). **That approach was abandoned** — on this VPS's disk it took
close to an hour per build, doubled disk usage to ~35GB for one file (a
raw copy plus a duplicate baked into the build cache), and once nearly
filled the disk on a box that also runs a production Postgres instance.

The corrected design **bind-mounts** the `.duckdb` file into the container
instead. The image build only ever touches app code and takes seconds;
updating data never requires a rebuild, and the file exists on disk
exactly once.

Also: the API originally lived at `147-251-255-246.sslip.io` (a magic-DNS
service needing zero setup). That was replaced with a real domain,
`geo-explorer.geomattr.org`, because `sslip.io` is categorized as
"Dynamic DNS" by common corporate/campus web filters (a FortiGate
appliance here) and got silently blocked on any network running that
filter — see the callout in §4 for the full story, which is still worth
reading since the debugging technique generalizes.
:::

Concrete values wired into the repo:

| Thing | Value |
|---|---|
| GitHub org/repo | `RegRed-project/geo_explorer_website` (note: renamed from `regred-project` mid-project — GitHub redirects, but update the git remote to avoid the redirect notice) |
| Pages URL | `https://regred-project.github.io/geo_explorer_website/` |
| VPS public IP | `147.251.255.246` |
| API hostname | `geo-explorer.geomattr.org` (Cloudflare DNS record, **DNS only** / grey-cloud — not proxied, so Caddy handles TLS directly) |

If any of these change, update: `backend/Caddyfile`, `frontend/js/app.js`
(`API_BASE`), `backend/app/main.py` (`allow_origins`), and the default host
in `deploy.sh`.

## 1. One-time: create the GitHub repo

```bash
git remote add origin git@github.com:RegRed-project/geo_explorer_website.git
git add .
git commit -m "Initial FastAPI + static frontend setup"
git push -u origin main
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Gotchas that actually came up here
- **GPG commit signing needs a real TTY.** If `git commit` fails with
  `gpg: signing failed: No passphrase given` or `gpg: cannot open '/dev/tty'`,
  run `export GPG_TTY=$(tty)` first, or (if signing truly can't work in your
  shell) commit with `git commit --no-gpg-sign` for that one commit.
- **GitHub blocks pushes that expose a private email (`GH007`).** If your
  account has "Block command line pushes that expose my email" enabled and
  your commit author uses your real email, the push is rejected. Fix by
  setting a repo-local git identity to your GitHub-provided noreply address
  before committing:
  ```bash
  git config user.email "<id>+<username>@users.noreply.github.com"
  git commit --amend --reset-author --no-edit --no-gpg-sign
  ```
  (find your exact noreply address at <https://github.com/settings/emails>).
- **If the remote already has commits that don't match local history**
  (e.g. you committed the old GHCR-based design and pushed it before this
  redesign), a normal push is rejected as non-fast-forward. Force-push
  deliberately once you're sure:
  ```bash
  git push --force-with-lease origin main
  ```
:::

In the repo: **Settings → Pages → Source → "GitHub Actions"**. This is
required — the `deploy-frontend.yml` workflow will run and even succeed
without it configured, but the site itself stays a 404 until Pages is
explicitly turned on this way.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Also check this if under an org
If pushes/workflows behave oddly (e.g. `GITHUB_TOKEN` can't push packages,
or Actions never trigger), the org may have Actions locked down by default:
check **Settings → Actions → General → Actions permissions** (must allow
workflows to run) and **Workflow permissions**. If "Read and write
permissions" is greyed out (common under an org), don't wait on an org
owner — see the GHCR note in the backend section below; for this project's
final design, no registry write access is needed at all, which sidesteps
the problem entirely.
:::

## 2. One-time: prepare the VPS (147.251.255.246)

SSH in and install Docker + the Compose plugin:

```bash
ssh gortega@147.251.255.246
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER   # log out/in after this
```

Create the deploy directory, owned by your user (`/opt` is root-owned by
default — this bit people the first time):

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /opt/geo-explorer
sudo chown $USER:$USER /opt/geo-explorer
```

Back on your machine, set up key-based SSH so `deploy.sh` doesn't prompt
for a password every time:

```bash
ssh-copy-id gortega@147.251.255.246
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Two separate firewalls, not one
Opening ports on the VPS's own OS firewall is **not** sufficient on cloud
infrastructure — there is usually also a cloud-level security group in
front of it, and both must allow inbound TCP 80/443 from `0.0.0.0/0`
(the whole internet, not just "my IP", which is a common console default
and will still block Let's Encrypt's validation servers even though it
looks open from your own machine).

```bash
# OS-level firewall (if ufw is in use)
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
```

Then, separately, check the cloud provider's console for a security group
/ network firewall on the VM and open TCP 80 and 443 there too, source
`0.0.0.0/0`.

**How this actually failed here**: after opening only what looked
sufficient, `curl` to the hostname timed out on both 80 and 443, while
`docker`/`caddy` on the box were confirmed listening (`ss -tlnp`). Testing
against the **raw IP** (bypassing a `sslip.io`-specific local network
filter that was a red herring) confirmed port 80 worked once the cloud
security group was actually opened to `0.0.0.0/0`.
:::

## 3. Deploy the backend

From the repo root, with `geographic_entities_prepared.duckdb` present on
disk (it's gitignored — it just needs to exist locally):

```bash
./deploy.sh
```

This does everything:

1. `rsync`s the repo to `/opt/geo-explorer` on the VPS (excludes `.git` and
   `frontend/`). rsync only re-transfers the `.duckdb` file if its content
   actually changed, so routine code-only deploys are fast (seconds).
2. SSHes in and runs `docker compose up -d --build`, which builds the
   (now tiny, code-only) `backend/Dockerfile` image and (re)starts both
   the `fastapi` and `caddy` containers. The data file is bind-mounted,
   not copied, so this step no longer touches the 17GB file at all.

Run `./deploy.sh` again any time you change backend code or the data file.
Pass a different target if needed: `./deploy.sh otheruser@otherhost`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What changed from the original design
`backend/Dockerfile` no longer has a `COPY` step for the `.duckdb` file.
`docker-compose.yml`'s `fastapi` service instead has:
```yaml
volumes:
  - ./geographic_entities_prepared.duckdb:/data/geographic_entities_prepared.duckdb:ro
```
`backend/app/config.py`'s `DB_PATH` already pointed at
`/data/geographic_entities_prepared.duckdb`, so no app code changed —
only how that path gets populated inside the container.
:::

### If a build/rsync is ever interrupted mid-way

Docker build cache from an aborted attempt can accumulate quickly with
large layers. If disk fills up:

```bash
ssh gortega@147.251.255.246 'docker builder prune -af && df -h /'
```

Also check for stale duplicates of the data file left over from earlier
manual attempts (e.g. inside `backend/` instead of the repo root) — the
current Dockerfile only ever reads
`geographic_entities_prepared.duckdb` at the repo root.

## 4. TLS certificate notes

Caddy obtains a Let's Encrypt certificate for `geo-explorer.geomattr.org`
automatically on first start, as long as the DNS record is **DNS only**
(grey cloud in Cloudflare, not proxied) and ports 80/443 are actually
reachable from the internet (§2).

::: {.callout-important}
## Why this domain instead of sslip.io, and a Cloudflare gotcha
The API originally lived at `147-251-255-246.sslip.io` — a magic-DNS
service that needs zero setup (the IP is embedded in the hostname). It
worked, but **`sslip.io` is categorized as "Dynamic DNS" by common
corporate/campus web filters** (confirmed here via a FortiGate appliance,
which returned an explicit "Category: Dynamic DNS" block page over plain
HTTP, and a fake `FortiGate CA`-issued certificate over HTTPS). Anyone
browsing from a network with that kind of filter would see the site as
broken, even though the server was fine. Moving to a real registered
domain isn't a workaround — it just doesn't trigger that categorization.

**If you point a domain at the VPS through Cloudflare**, make sure the
record is set to **DNS only**, not **Proxied**. A proxied record resolves
to Cloudflare's edge IPs instead of your VPS, so Let's Encrypt's HTTP-01
challenge (and Caddy's own automatic HTTPS) will try to validate against
Cloudflare, not your origin — Caddy's own cert issuance won't complete
correctly. (If you *want* Cloudflare's proxy/CDN, that's a different,
valid setup — but it means letting Cloudflare terminate TLS at its edge
with its own certificate instead of Caddy's, e.g. Cloudflare "Full"
mode — this project didn't need that, so it uses DNS only.)

Also: DNS changes at Cloudflare take effect immediately, but *your own
local resolver's cache* won't reflect that until its TTL expires. If a
DNS change "isn't working," query a public resolver directly before
assuming anything is broken:
```bash
dig @1.1.1.1 +short geo-explorer.geomattr.org A
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## If certificate issuance stalls or the chain fails to verify for some clients
- If ports were closed (or DNS was still pointing at Cloudflare's proxy)
  when Caddy first tried and it's now sitting in a retry backoff (Caddy
  logs `will retry ... retrying_in: <n>`), don't wait it out — force an
  immediate retry: `docker compose restart caddy`.
- Caddy's default certificate is **ECDSA**, chaining through a newer
  Let's Encrypt root. Every modern browser trusts it, but some
  older/vendored CA bundles (used by some non-browser HTTP clients) don't
  yet. For maximum compatibility this project forces RSA instead, in
  `backend/Caddyfile`:
  ```
  geo-explorer.geomattr.org {
      tls {
          key_type rsa2048
      }
      reverse_proxy fastapi:8000
  }
  ```
  Changing this setting does **not** retroactively reissue an
  already-valid cached certificate. Force reissuance by deleting the
  cached cert and restarting:
  ```bash
  docker compose exec caddy rm -rf \
    "/data/caddy/certificates/acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org-directory/geo-explorer.geomattr.org"
  docker compose restart caddy
  ```
- To sanity-check the served chain independent of any network weirdness,
  check from the VPS itself over loopback:
  ```bash
  echo | openssl s_client -connect localhost:443 -servername geo-explorer.geomattr.org \
    2>&1 | grep -E "^Certificate chain|^ [0-9]+ s:|Verify return code"
  ```
  `Verify return code: 0 (ok)` means the chain is genuinely fine, even if
  a specific test client elsewhere fails to validate it.
:::

## 5. Deploy the frontend

Push to `main` with changes under `frontend/` — `deploy-frontend.yml`
publishes `frontend/` to GitHub Pages automatically. No build step, no
secrets, runs on a standard hosted runner.

Confirm it actually deployed (not just that the workflow ran):

```bash
curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/RegRed-project/geo_explorer_website/pages
```

A `404` here means Pages was never turned on in Settings (see step 1) —
the workflow can report success while this still 404s, so check both.

## 6. Verify end-to-end

```bash
# API is reachable and has a valid cert
curl https://geo-explorer.geomattr.org/api/tables

# CORS is configured for the Pages origin
curl -I -H "Origin: https://regred-project.github.io" \
  https://geo-explorer.geomattr.org/api/tables | grep -i access-control

# Full site
open https://regred-project.github.io/geo_explorer_website/
```

In the browser: pick a table, filter to a single row, and confirm the
table and the Leaflet map both render.

::: {.callout-note}
## If your own `curl`/tooling can't validate the cert but a browser can
This happened during development: a local institutional network was
running SSL inspection (a Fortinet appliance presenting its own MITM
certificate for the `sslip.io` domain specifically), and a separate
automated fetch tool had an outdated root-certificate bundle missing the
current Let's Encrypt root. Both gave misleading failures despite the
server being correctly configured (confirmed via `openssl s_client`
loopback on the VPS itself, per step 4). If in doubt, trust a real
browser's judgment over a CLI tool's, and verify server-side via loopback
before assuming the deployment is broken.
:::

## Updating the data later

1. Replace `geographic_entities_prepared.duckdb` locally with the new
   version.
2. `./deploy.sh`

The new file gets rsynced up and `deploy.sh` explicitly restarts the
`fastapi` container so it picks it up — no image rebuild needed for data
alone.

::: {.callout-important}
## Why the explicit restart matters
`docker compose up -d --build` only recreates a container when its image
or compose config changed — it does **not** notice that a bind-mounted
file's *content* changed on disk, since from Compose's point of view
nothing about the container's configuration is different. Without an
explicit restart, `fastapi` keeps running with the DuckDB connection it
opened at startup and silently keeps serving the *old* data indefinitely,
even though the file on disk (and the API's own `docker compose ps`
output) looks completely normal. `deploy.sh` runs
`docker compose restart fastapi` after every `up -d --build` specifically
to guard against this — if you ever deploy some other way, remember to
restart `fastapi` yourself after a data update.
:::

## Troubleshooting summary

- **Website shows old data after updating `geographic_entities_prepared.duckdb`
  and running `./deploy.sh`**: see the callout just above — this means
  `fastapi` wasn't restarted. Check `docker compose ps` for its uptime; if
  it's older than your deploy, run
  `docker compose restart fastapi` on the VPS by hand.
- **`./deploy.sh` hangs or asks for a password every time**: SSH key auth
  isn't set up — rerun `ssh-copy-id gortega@147.251.255.246`.
- **Build/deploy is extremely slow or disk fills up**: confirm you're on
  the bind-mount design (§3), not an older `COPY`-the-file-into-the-image
  version — that design was abandoned for exactly this reason.
- **Caddy cert fails to issue / times out**: check *both* the OS firewall
  and the cloud provider's security group for ports 80/443, open to
  `0.0.0.0/0` (§2). If ports were fixed after Caddy already tried and
  failed, `docker compose restart caddy` to retry immediately instead of
  waiting for its backoff timer.
- **A cert seems invalid to some client but not others**: verify server-side
  via `openssl s_client` loopback (§4) before assuming it's actually
  broken — client-side CA bundles and local network SSL inspection can
  both produce false negatives.
- **CORS errors in the browser console**: the `Origin` header the browser
  sends must exactly match an entry in `allow_origins` in
  `backend/app/main.py` (scheme + host only, no path) — run `./deploy.sh`
  again after changing it.
- **GitHub Pages shows a 404**: confirm Settings → Pages → Source is set
  to "GitHub Actions" (§1) — a green `deploy-frontend.yml` run does not by
  itself mean Pages is turned on; check
  `curl https://api.github.com/repos/<org>/<repo>/pages` for a 404.
- **`git push` rejected (email privacy / GH007, or non-fast-forward)**:
  see the callout in §1.

## Reference: the files that make this work

`deploy.sh` (repo root, executable):

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Deploys the backend to the VPS: syncs the repo, then builds and restarts
# the containers over SSH. No GitHub Actions, no container registry.
#
# Usage: ./deploy.sh [user@host]
# Defaults to VPS_HOST below if no argument is given.
set -euo pipefail

VPS="${1:-gortega@147.251.255.246}"
REMOTE_DIR="/opt/geo-explorer"

echo "==> Syncing repo to $VPS:$REMOTE_DIR (the .duckdb file only re-transfers if it changed)"
rsync -avz --info=progress2 \
  --exclude '.git' \
  --exclude 'frontend' \
  --exclude '__pycache__' \
  ./ "$VPS:$REMOTE_DIR/"

echo "==> Building and restarting containers on $VPS"
# `up -d --build` only recreates a container when its image or compose
# config changed — it does NOT notice that the bind-mounted .duckdb file's
# *content* changed, so fastapi would otherwise keep serving from its
# already-open connection to the old data indefinitely. Always restart it
# explicitly so data updates actually take effect.
ssh "$VPS" "cd $REMOTE_DIR && docker compose up -d --build && docker compose restart fastapi"

echo "==> Done. Check: curl https://geo-explorer.geomattr.org/api/tables"
```

`docker-compose.yml` (repo root):

```yaml
services:
  fastapi:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: backend/Dockerfile
    restart: unless-stopped
    expose:
      - "8000"
    volumes:
      - ./geographic_entities_prepared.duckdb:/data/geographic_entities_prepared.duckdb:ro

  caddy:
    image: caddy:2-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - ./backend/Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro
      - caddy_data:/data
      - caddy_config:/config
    depends_on:
      - fastapi

volumes:
  caddy_data:
  caddy_config:
```

`backend/Dockerfile`:

```dockerfile
# Built directly on the VPS (docker compose build) — no registry involved.
# Build context is the repo root (see ../docker-compose.yml), so paths below
# are relative to the repo root, not this file's directory.
#
# The .duckdb file is NOT copied into the image — it's bind-mounted at
# runtime (see docker-compose.yml). That keeps the image small and the
# build fast/instant regardless of data size, and means updating the data
# never requires a rebuild, just a container restart.
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /srv

COPY backend/requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY backend/app/ ./app/

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
```

`backend/Caddyfile`:

```
geo-explorer.geomattr.org {
	tls {
		key_type rsa2048
	}
	reverse_proxy fastapi:8000
}
```
